key_gap: Both sides chose the same class of counter — targeted, time-boxed, reversible (90-day 15-20% renewal discount + onboarding credit for the top-60 at-risk accounts) — but the human decided in 72 hours at ~60% information, while the AI's WHY/HOW verification loop consumed the tempo budget and its decision landed at T+6 days, outside the 72-hour window. In this market the first mover in each pricing round sets the frame sales carries into the renewal conversations, so a correct answer that ships late is a correct answer that loses: the human treated the decision deadline as a first-class decision variable derived from the market clock (T+14 conversations); the AI treated it as a constraint to note and spend.
learning_signal: In tempo markets, the decision deadline and loop cadence are first-class decision variables on equal footing with content correctness. Derive the deadline from the market clock (renewal dates, contract dates, conversation start dates), not from analysis availability; decide at the information level the deadline allows (~60% here) and price the residual uncertainty rather than studying it; keep the response targeted, time-boxed, and sized against the competitor's burn capacity so the war is not extended; reopen analysis in the next loop (T+30 re-observation trigger), not inside the current one.
suggested_improvement: Add a tempo gate in META/HOW: (a) before any stage, compute the decision deadline from the market clock and the stage budget against it; (b) insert a 'decide now at current information' check before each verification pass — if verification would push the decision past the deadline, truncate it and record the truncation; (c) require every alternative to state its execution lead time and deadline impact; (d) after selection, emit an explicit re-observation trigger (next loop point) so analysis resumes at the correct cadence.

key_gap: The pure style converted every competitor probe into a same-week reactive counter — 5 moves, 5 responses (20 bps margin given on all new signups, two engineering quarters on payroll parity, one on dev-portal parity, six months of free-reader hardware, a marketing blitz) — while churn held flat at 1.2% (closure-driven, no competitive-poaching trend) because Meridian's moat (14-year POS-vendor exclusives, certification, terminal switching costs) locked the installed base, and the POS-vendor integration project — the only moat bridge — was starved to three quarters behind schedule. The AI re-routed META from 'competitor moved — respond fast' to structural analysis, classified all five moves as probes against the moat (evidence: churn data and the fact that GridStone already wins the contested segment on velocity), responded once, time-boxed (60-day free-reader match, highest-converting cohort), preserved the moat engineering, and scheduled the decisive engagement to the T+9 switching event (contract-expiry cluster) — tempo only pays when it moves an outcome the competitor can feel.
learning_signal: Tempo is only an advantage when it moves an outcome the competitor can feel; against a structural moat (contractual exclusives, certification, switching costs), reactive tempo converts into margin and engineering burn with zero churn impact. Before responding to any competitor move: (a) identify the moat and its mechanisms first; (b) classify the move as probe vs. equilibrium-changing — a probe is a move whose response cannot change the outcome (its target is locked by switching costs, or you already win there), using churn/flow data as the falsifying evidence; (c) cap reactive responses and time-box any that ship; (d) time the real engagement to the switching event (contract expiries, certification lapses) rather than the competitor's probe cadence.
suggested_improvement: Add a moat screen between WHY and HOW: (a) name the structural moat and its mechanisms before evaluating any competitor move; (b) require a probe-vs-equilibrium classification per move with cited evidence (churn data, switching costs, who wins the contested segment today); (c) gate every proposed response on 'does this change a competitor-observable outcome?' with reject + reason recorded otherwise; (d) maintain a moat-investment ledger whose engineering allocation is protected from parity work; (e) schedule response windows at switching events (contract/certification calendars) instead of reacting to probe cadence.
